title: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals the target, and count the number of ways.
shortTitle: Target Sum — assign + and - signs to reach a target

s1_definition.profdef: Transform into subset-sum counting. If P is the subset assigned plus and N the subset assigned minus, then P−N=target and P+N=total, so P=(total+target)/2. Count subsets summing to that value with dp[s] += dp[s−num]. Valid only if total+target is non-negative and even. Time O(n · P), space O(P).
s1_definition.analogy: An adjustment clerk at National Bank of India must mark each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net equals a required figure, and wants to know how many sign assignments work. This equals choosing which amounts become credits, so it reduces to counting subsets that hit a fixed total.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Transform into subset-sum counting. If P is the subset assigned plus and N the subset assigned minus, then P−N=target and P+N=total, so P=(total+target)/2. Count subsets summing to that value with dp[s] += dp[s−num]. Valid only if total+target is non-negative and even. Time O(n · P), space O(P).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An adjustment clerk at National Bank of India must mark each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net equals a required figure, and wants to know how many sign assignments work. This equals choosing which amounts become credits, so it reduces to counting subsets that hit a fixed total.

**One line to remember:** P=(total+target)/2; count subsets summing to P; dp[s] += dp[s−num].

sections.s2_technical:
Let the positive subset sum be P and the negative subset sum be N. Then P minus N is the target and P plus N is the total, so adding the two equations gives P equals (total plus target) divided by two. If total plus target is negative or odd, no assignment works, so return zero.

Now the problem is: how many subsets sum to P. Use a one-dimensional counting dp where dp[s] is the number of subsets summing to s, with dp[0]=1, sweeping s downward for each number: `for (int s = P; s >= num; s--) dp[s] += dp[s - num];`. The downward sweep keeps each number used once. The answer is dp[P].

The time is O(n · P) and space is O(P). A senior nuance is handling the edge where a number is zero: a zero can be assigned either sign without changing the sum, which the subset-count naturally accounts for since dp[0] already includes the empty choice and zeros simply double counts through the standard recurrence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an adjustment clerk marks each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net adjustment equals a required figure, and wants the number of valid sign assignments. This is exactly how Target Sum works.

Problem 2 — Enumerating all two-to-the-n sign combinations is infeasible for many amounts. This is exactly why the problem is reduced to a subset-sum count.

The mini-project builds an `AdjustmentCounter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input amounts are five ones with target three.

Step 1: The total is five, and total plus target is eight, which is even, so the positive-subset target P is four.

Step 2: dp of zero is one and all other sums start at zero.

Step 3: Processing each one shifts counts upward, building the number of subsets that sum to each value.

Step 4: After all five ones, dp of four counts the subsets of size four from five ones, which is five.

Step 5: The answer is five valid sign assignments, and the single-one target-two case has odd total-plus-target so it returns zero.

```text
2026-10-27T04:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Adjustment Counter (Target Sum)
2026-10-27T04:00:00Z [INFO] Valid sign assignments = 5
2026-10-27T04:00:00Z [INFO] {1,1,1,1,1}, target 3 → 5
2026-10-27T04:00:00Z [WARNING] No valid sign assignment exists
2026-10-27T04:00:00Z [INFO] {1}, target 2 → 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  amounts={1,1,1,1,1} target=3 total=5
  P=(total+target)/2=(5+3)/2=4
  dp[0]=1 ; for each 1: dp[s]+=dp[s-1] DOWNWARD
  dp[4] = C(5,4) = 5   ← answer
  (total+target odd or negative ⇒ 0)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Target Sum asks how many ways I can assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals a target, and the elegant move is to transform it into a subset-sum count. If I call the plus-signed subset P and the minus-signed subset N, then P minus N is the target and P plus N is the total. Adding those equations gives P equal to the total plus the target, all divided by two.

So I first check feasibility: if the total plus the target is negative or odd, then P would be fractional or impossible and the answer is zero. Otherwise the question becomes how many subsets sum to P, which I count with a one-dimensional counting dynamic programming array. I set dp of zero to one and for each number sweep sums downward adding dp of the sum minus the number, so each number is used once. The answer is dp of P.

In my project at National Bank of India, an adjustment clerk marked each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net adjustment equaled a required figure and wanted the number of valid assignments. Enumerating two-to-the-n combinations was infeasible, so I reduced it to this subset-sum count that runs in time proportional to the number of amounts times the target subset sum.
